<reason>PRO built a coherent story about hierarchy and humiliation, and its point that attachment to the currency can coexist with collapsing trust in fairness was its strongest live route. But CON systematically converted the clash into a falsifiability contest and won it: it showed PRO's motive-theory relabels every act of giving, offered concrete facts (2012 haircut then continued forbearance, the September 2015 re-election with rupture parties on the ballot, the swift 2020 joint-borrowing proposal), and in B4.1 answered PRO's pressure question with five specific outcomes that would have proven the motion. PRO's closing simply reasserted that CON's test "cannot lose" without engaging those five outcomes, and PRO's own A2 concession about Italian spreads was turned into evidence of shared fate. CON also handled the pandemic-timing objection plausibly (blameless shock as ordinary condition of democratic consent). CON's clipped final turn is a small execution cost, but it made the decisive comparison—distrust that changes conduct versus distrust that loses every real decision—clearer and harder to resist.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.3–B2.6 and B4.1: CON showed that forbearance continued after private exposure was gone, that Greeks re-elected the signing government over explicit exit parties, and then, when pressed on whether its test could ever lose, listed five concrete falsifying outcomes that never occurred—pressure PRO's closing left unanswered.</best_rebuttal>
